📡 NuModem EG800 User Manual

Drive a 4G modem from your browser — AT commands, live annotations, 18 languages

V26.0.76
Intro Requirements Quick Start Power-Up Ritual Terminal Signal Bar AT Panel Ten Tabs Test Method FAQ

🎯 Introduction

NuModem EG800 is a 4G modem console in a single HTML file. It sends AT commands straight to Quectel EG800K series modules through the browser's Web Serial API — nothing to install, no software beyond the USB driver, and no backend server.

What makes it different from an ordinary serial terminal? It understands AT commands. Every command you send and every line the module sends back gets a plain-language explanation attached in real time — including the error codes that are nothing but a number.

What this manual covers
From opening the page, hooking up the module and running the power-up ritual, all the way through the working principle and test procedure for every AT command group in all ten function tabs. Every behaviour described here comes from hands-on testing of a physical EG800K in August 2026, not from copying the manual — where the manual is wrong, this document says so.

Language and theme

💻 System Requirements

Browser

NuModem is built on the Web Serial API, which only exists in Chromium-based browsers.

BrowserVersionStatus
Google Chrome89 or later✅ Recommended
Microsoft Edge89 or later✅ Supported
Opera75 or later✅ Supported
Firefox—❌ No Web Serial API
Safari—❌ No Web Serial API
Opening it straight from file:// works — Chromium treats local files as a secure origin, so Web Serial is not blocked. Download it, double-click NuModem_EG800.html and connect; serving it over https:// or http://localhost works just as well. The only difference is that fetch() is blocked by CORS under file:// — but the translation files are loaded with <script> tags, so all 18 languages still work.

Hardware

ItemDetails
ModuleQuectel EG800K series (all measurements in this document were taken on firmware EG800KCNGCR07A06M04)
InterfaceUSB-UART bridge. Testing used a CH343 (1A86:55D3)
Baud rate115200
Line endingCR (send LF and the module answers nothing at all)
SIM cardOnly needed for data features. Testing used a 1NCE IoT SIM with an auto-assigned APN

The control board must be able to switch module power with RTS and drive the Reset pin with DTR, otherwise the power-up ritual is impossible (see Power-Up Ritual).

🚀 Quick Start

Step 1 — Open NuModem

Open NuModem_EG800.html in Chrome or Edge — a double-click is enough, no server needed.

Step 2 — Connect the module

Click Connect in the top left. The browser pops up a port picker; choose your USB-UART bridge. The arrow on the right expands a dropdown so you can pick a previously authorized port directly.

Once a port has been authorized, clicking "Connect" on later visits attaches to it immediately without asking again. If you have several serial devices, the dropdown is faster.

Step 3 — Check the baud rate

The baud rate selector at the top defaults to 115200, which is the EG800K factory value, so you normally leave it alone.

Step 4 — Run the power-up ritual

Do not skip this step. The instant the browser opens the serial port it re-asserts RTS, and on this control board RTS is an active-low power switch — meaning the module loses power at the exact moment you connect. Details in the next section.

The classic symptom of skipping the power-up ritual is this: the terminal shows every command you send, but nothing ever comes back. That is not a wrong baud rate and not swapped wires — the module simply has no power.

🔌 The Power-Up Ritual (the most important section)

The EG800K does not boot just because it has power. This control board wires two RS-232 output signals to the module's control pins:

SignalWired toLogic
RTSModule power switch Active low: RTS OFF = powered, RTS ON = powered off
DTRModule Reset pin DTR ON = Reset held high (can boot), OFF = Reset pulled low

Standard procedure

Switch to the Hardware tab, which has two dedicated buttons:

  1. Power — walks RTS through ON → OFF once. The button turns green when power is on (that is, RTS is OFF).
    ⚠ Setting OFF directly does not guarantee power; you must go ON first, then OFF.
  2. Wait one second.
  3. Reset — this is a press-and-hold button: pressing pulls DTR to OFF, releasing returns it to ON. Hold for roughly 300 ms.
  4. Wait for RDY in the terminal. In testing it appears within a few seconds.

You can also click RTS / DTR on the signal bar directly — same effect, you just have to keep track of the sequence yourself.

How to confirm the module booted

The terminal should spit out this sequence:

RDY              ← module boot complete
+CFUN: 1         ← RF enabled
+CPIN: READY     ← SIM ready
+QUSIM: 1
+QIND: SMS DONE  ← SMS initialization complete
+QIND: PB DONE   ← phonebook initialization complete

Then send ATI to verify: you should get three lines — manufacturer, model, firmware revision — plus OK.

⚠ Every page reload requires running the power-up ritual again. Reloading reopens the serial port, and reopening the serial port re-asserts RTS — which cuts power to the module all over again. This is the number one reason people conclude "the module is dead" when using this tool.

Two commands worth sending right after boot

CommandWhy
ATE1 Turns echo on. The module echoes back every command it receives verbatim, so the terminal lets you compare "what you sent" against "what the module actually received" — typos become obvious at a glance.
AT+CMEE=2 Switches error messages to verbose text. Without it, failures are just a bare ERROR; with it you get readable messages like +CME ERROR: SIM not inserted.

Both are session-only and must be re-sent after the module reboots.

🔴 When no URC ever arrives, the first thing to check is AT+QURCCFG="urcport". The factory setting routes URCs (unsolicited result codes) to the USB AT port, so this tool — which talks over UART — never sees a single one. The symptom is "every command returns OK but nothing else ever happens": GNSS fixes, TCP data arrival, MQTT messages and Wi-Fi scan results all stay silent. Fix: AT+QURCCFG="urcport","uart1", which writes to NVRAM and survives reboots.

📟 Terminal

The right half is the terminal. Its biggest difference from an ordinary serial terminal is that every line is annotated.

Four colors

ColorMeaning
TXData you sent
RXData returned by the module
SYSThe tool's own system messages (connection, signal changes, entering/leaving data mode)
CMTAnnotations — the explanations that start with //

All four colors are customizable; click a color swatch to open the picker.

The annotation engine

This is the heart of NuModem. It does two things:

  • Explains the command you send — send AT+QSSLSEND=4,18 and the annotation reads "send a fixed length of 18 bytes on clientID 4: after the module prints the > prompt you must send exactly 18 bytes for it to transmit; no Ctrl+Z required".
  • Decodes the module's responses — especially the purely numeric codes. For example +QFTPSIZE: 627,550 is split into two layers: "error 627: FTP did not perform the requested action; server replied 550: action not taken, file or directory not found".
Annotations follow the parameters you actually entered. Fill the same button with different values and the numbers in the annotation change with them — it is not canned help text.

Line ending

The line ending selector sits to the right of the input box. The EG800K requires CR; choose LF and the module answers nothing at all. This is the easiest setting to get wrong.

Other

  • The bottom shows cumulative RX / TX byte counts and the current port name.
  • A row of buttons in the top right: annotation toggle, line ending, timestamp, auto-scroll, clear.
  • The terminal area also has Satellites and Map tabs, which fill in once GNSS obtains a fix.

🚦 RS-232 Signal Bar

Once connected, a row of signal lamps appears below the title bar, split into two groups.

LOCAL (OUT) — your outputs, clickable

SignalPurpose on this board
BRKBreak signal
RTSModule power (active low, OFF = powered)
DTRModule Reset (ON = Reset held high)

REMOTE (IN) — the module's outputs, read-only

DCD / DSR / CTS / RI, plus two indicators: ACT (data flowing) and ERR (framing/parity error).

Web Serial cannot read back the state of the signals you assert. So those three LOCAL lamps show "the value this tool believes it sent", not a hardware read-back. To confirm an action really took effect, trust the terminal's system messages (things like RTS → ON).

🎛️ How the AT Command Panel Works

The left half holds ten tabs and over two hundred buttons. Before looking at individual tabs, understand these shared mechanisms — they apply on every page.

Two kinds of buttons

StyleBehaviour
Plain buttonClicking sends immediately
Dashed outlineHas parameters to fill in. Once filled you can "Send", or "Insert into command line" to drop the assembled command into the input box below and edit it yourself

Parameter fields

Every field has its own description (hover to see it) stating the range measured on real hardware, not copied from the manual. For example, the Wi-Fi scan "rounds" field says 1-3, because that is what AT+QWIFISCAN=? actually returns — the 1-6 printed in the application note is wrong.

Two-stage data send

Some commands do not finish in a single line. Their flow is:

Send command  →  module replies > or CONNECT  →  send exactly N bytes  →  module returns the result

Buttons of this kind have a separate "data payload" field, and the length is computed automatically and inserted into the command, so you never count bytes yourself. The commands in this category are AT+QISEND, AT+QSSLSEND, AT+QMTPUBEX, AT+QHTTPURL, AT+QHTTPPOST and AT+QFTPPUT.

Getting the length wrong is ugly. The module keeps waiting until it has received exactly the number of bytes you declared, and during that time the AT port is in "data mode" — anything else you type gets swallowed as payload.

How to escape: send an ESC (0x1B) with the raw-byte button on the Hardware tab. No need to disconnect, no need to reboot the module.

Escape sequences

The data payload field is a single-line text box, so you cannot type newlines, tabs or other control characters. These fields therefore support escape sequences:

NotationByte sent
\n0x0A line feed
\r0x0D carriage return
\t0x09 tab
\00x00 NUL
\xHHAny byte, HH in hexadecimal
\\A literal backslash

Decoding happens before transmission, and the length is computed from the decoded byte count. For example hello\n is 7 characters in the field but 6 bytes on the wire, so the length written into the command is 6.

Why this matters: many test servers echo line by line (they return whatever you send, but only act once they see a newline). If your payload does not end with \n, you will never receive a response — and it will look exactly like a broken connection.

Timeout markers

Some AT commands block for a long time. The ⏱ marker on a button is the maximum wait time stated in the manual, for example AT+QIACT=1 up to 150 seconds, AT+COPS=? up to 300 seconds. When something seems unresponsive, check this marker first — usually the time simply has not elapsed yet.

Confirmation dialogs

A confirmation box appears only for actions that can strand the AT port in data mode, or that are irreversible (deleting a remote file, soft-restarting the module, changing the baud rate). Merely "this will consume data" does not block you — that kind of warning lives in the button's description instead.

Local toggles

A few buttons have a small checkbox underneath. That is a tool-side behaviour, not an AT command. For example, under AT+QICLOSE=0 there is "auto-close when +QIURC: "closed",0 is detected". These options are stored in the browser and persist across sessions.

🗂️ The Ten Tabs

The tab order is meaningful: left to right is roughly the order you should work in. Hardware to power up → Basic to confirm the module is alive → Network to confirm it can get online → the last five are the various data protocols.

Hardware — Power-up and the serial port

Working principle: this page is the foundation of the whole tool: Control holds the two buttons of the power-up ritual (Power / Reset), Module is product identification, Serial is the UART settings, Power is low-power mode, URC governs the output port for the module's unsolicited messages, and a row of raw-byte buttons (Ctrl+Z / ESC / +++) serves as the escape hatch out of data mode. Every other tab rests on two premises: the module was powered up by the ritual and URCs go to uart1 — both are taken care of on this page. Every behavior and number in this section was measured on a physical EG800K in August 2026.

Why there is a power-up ritual: RTS = power, DTR = Reset

The control board this tool pairs with repurposes two RS-232 handshake signals; this is the key to the whole page:

SignalActually wired toLogic
RTSModule power switch Negative logic: RTS OFF = powered, RTS ON = power cut
DTRModule Reset pin DTR ON = Reset pulled high (can boot), DTR OFF = Reset pulled low

Circuit behavior (confirmed by testing): on the first connection RTS must go ON first, then OFF, or the power will not actually turn on — setting it straight to OFF does not guarantee power; DTR likewise must walk ON→OFF→ON before Reset is truly pulled high. A power cut (RTS ON) is a hard cut — the module sends no farewell message whatsoever.

Reloading the page = a power cut. When the browser reopens the serial port it raises RTS again, and the module simply loses power — after the automatic reconnect completes you must rerun the power-up ritual. Stepped on in testing: skipping the ritual and sending 17 commands straight away, every one vanished into the void (TX lines only, zero RX). Any "it was fine a moment ago, now nothing responds" — think of this first.

The Power and Reset buttons: how to press them, what you will see

The two buttons are the embodiment of the two signals in the table above, and they are linked both ways with the RTS / DTR indicators in the signal bar (grayed out and unclickable while disconnected). Web Serial cannot read back the actual state of output signals; what the signal bar shows is the value this tool believes it has sent.

  1. Power (toggle): lit green = power ON (= RTS OFF). The power-up ritual requires RTS to pass through ON→OFF: if the button is already lit, click it off first, then on.
  2. Reset (momentary): press = DTR OFF, release = DTR ON — one press-and-release is one Reset (the standard sequence pauses 0.3 seconds in between).
  3. Wait for RDY: within a few seconds the terminal shows the module's boot announcement RDY.
  4. Verify with ATI: it should reply Quectel / EG800K / Revision: … / OK. If that comes back, both the UART and the module are alive.
After power-up, first confirm echo (ATE) is on (the factory default is on), then send AT+CMEE=2 — without it you only get a bare ERROR; with it you get the readable text of +CME ERROR: …. Both are session-only and must be re-sent every time the module restarts.

Module: five identification buttons

ButtonCommandWhat you will see
InfoATI Vendor / model / firmware version, three in one — make it the first command after power-up
Vendor / Model / FW Ver AT+GMI / AT+GMM / AT+GMR The three lines of ATI queried separately (each equivalent to CGMI / CGMM / CGMR). Firmware version measured on this unit: EG800KCNGCR07A06M04
IMEIAT+GSN The module's IMEI (15 digits). Zero data cost, safe to send anytime

Serial: AT&V reads the parameters, IPR changes the baud rate

AT Params (AT&V): lists the current values of all single-letter AT parameters. The single-letter commands ATE / ATQ / ATV have no query form of their own; this is the only command that can read them. Measured on this unit: E:1 Q:0 V:1 S3:13 S4:10 — echo on, result codes in text mode, line ending = CR (ASCII 13), which is exactly what this tool's response parsing relies on.

Baud? (AT+IPR?): queries the UART's current baud rate; factory default 115200.
Baud List (AT+IPR=?): returns two lists — the first is the auto-detectable baud rates, the second those usable only in fixed mode. After you run this button, the Set Baud dropdown is replaced by the list this unit actually reported. Measured here, the second list runs all the way up to 1000000 bps — a value absent from the table in manual §3.4.

Set Baud (AT+IPR={rate};&W, parameter card): clicking it pops a confirmation dialog first — this is the button on the whole page most likely to lock you out.

The triple trap of changing the baud rate (all confirmed by testing):
① The moment OK comes back it takes effect immediately, and from the next instant this tool and the module are talking past each other;
② AT&F (factory reset) does not restore the baud rate — do not count on it to save you;
③ Without &W nothing is saved — and reconnecting = a power cut, so the module wakes at the old baud rate while your port setting is stuck at the new one: lost in both directions. That is why this tool enforces the combined ;&W form.
Four recovery steps (the confirmation dialog reminds you too): disconnect → change the baud rate in the connection area → reconnect → rerun the power-up ritual.

Power: QSCLK low-power mode

Sleep? (AT+QSCLK?): asks whether the module is allowed to sleep. Measured factory value on this unit: 0 = disabled, module always awake. This page provides the query button only: a sleeping module stops answering AT, and the manual's wake-up method is pulling DTR low — but on this board DTR is already wired as the Reset pin (see the start of this section). If you enabled sleep yourself on the command line and now cannot wake it, rerun the power-up ritual (power cycle) to escape; see the official low-power application note for details.

URC: when messages stop arriving, come here first

A URC (Unsolicited Result Code) is a message the module emits on its own, unprompted — it is the reply to no command. The boot-time RDY, TCP data arrival, MQTT messages, Wi-Fi scan results, and the GNSS firmware-load notice are all URCs. Their output port defaults from the factory to the USB port (usbat) — this tool, on the UART, receives none of them, and the symptom is textbook: every command replies OK, yet the messages never come.

ButtonCommandPurpose
URC Port?AT+QURCCFG="urcport" Asks where URCs currently go — when URCs are missing, query this first; it must return "uart1" for you to receive them
URC PortsAT+QURCCFG=? Which output ports this unit supports. Measured reply: ("usbat","usbmodem","uart1") — no "all" as mentioned in the manual (the manual notes some models lack it)
URC → UARTAT+QURCCFG="urcport","uart1" Switches to the main UART. Written to NVRAM, survives reboots — change it once and you are done
URC SwitchAT+QINDCFG="all" The URC master switch, the other big reason for "no URCs". Measured factory value on this unit is 1 (on); the problem is almost always the output port

The raw-byte buttons: the escape hatch out of data mode

Quite a few commands are two-stage: send the command, wait for the module's > prompt, then send the payload. Once inside this data mode, the module swallows every character you type as data — including the AT commands you meant to send. When the length is miscounted, you change your mind halfway, or a command jams, ordinary keys cannot save you; you need this row of buttons that each send a single raw byte:

ButtonSendsWhen to use it
Ctrl+Z0x1A Data mode's terminator: actually sends off what has been accumulated
ESC0x1B Cancels data mode and discards the accumulated content. The first choice for escape when a two-stage command jams and the AT port stops answering (manual §2.3.8)
+++Three + signs (raw bytes) Escapes from transparent data mode (such as FTP's COM: transfer) back to AT mode. The rules are strict: 1 second of silence before and after, and absolutely no CR/LF — measured: adding a CR renders it ineffective. It must be sent with this button, never typed on the command line
Testing overturns the manual: +++ is "abort", not "pause". The FTPS application note v1.5, page 13, says that after +++ you can return to data mode with ATO and resume the transfer; on the real device ATO only replies NO CARRIER — the transfer has already been aborted. Treat +++ as an emergency brake; do not expect to keep driving after pulling it.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
No response to any command Check the three suspects in order: ① the power-up ritual was not run (after a page reload it is always this); ② the line ending is set to LF — the module only accepts CR, LF gets zero response; ③ baud-rate mismatch (see the four recovery steps)
Pressed Reset but RDY never comes First check whether the Power button is lit — with no power, pressing Reset any number of times does nothing; on the first connection the power must pass through ON→OFF
Commands all reply OK, but URCs never arrive Odds are urcport is still at the factory usbat: click URC Port? to check, URC → UART to change; failing that, check the URC Switch master switch
The AT port suddenly "swallows commands"; nothing you type gets a response You are stuck in data mode and everything you type is being consumed as data — press ESC to escape

Basic — SIM, diagnostics and basic status

Working principle: this page is the starting point after every connection. Once the power-up ritual is done and the terminal shows RDY, come here first to do three things: switch error messages to a readable format, confirm the SIM is ready, and identify whose card this is. Except for AT&F and PIN / PUK unlocking, the entire page is read-only queries — clicking them does not change the module's state; the commands that touch connection state live in the Network, TCP/IP and other tabs. All samples in this section are values measured in August 2026 on a physical EG800K (firmware EG800KCNGCR07A06M04).

After power-up: RDY does not mean the SIM is ready

RDY is the URC the module sends on its own when it finishes booting. It only means the AT interface is alive; the SIM card is still slowly initializing behind it. Measured: sending SIM-related commands the moment RDY appears returns +CME ERROR: 14 (SIM busy) or even +CME ERROR: 13 (SIM failure); wait about 6 seconds and everything works.

When writing automation scripts, do not treat RDY as the "clear to start" signal. Pick one of two correct approaches: leave a fixed buffer of about 6 seconds after RDY; or poll AT+QINISTAT and proceed only once bit 1 (CPIN ready) is set.

Echo (ATE): "module echo" and "terminal local echo" are two different things

Echo is the module sending back verbatim the characters you sent it (ATE1 on, ATE0 off); the terminal's local echo is the tool side printing what you type onto the screen itself. The two switches are independent: with both on, every character appears twice.

  • This page's echo toggle button switches module echo with a single click. The boot default is on (corroborated by the measured AT parameter E:1).
  • The state shown on the button is not remembered out of thin air — the tool self-corrects from the actual responses (receiving an echoed line counts as on); if you hand-type ATE0 / ATE1 / AT&F on the command line, the button's state follows along and never drifts.
  • The toggle is session-only: a module restart returns it to the default. To make it the boot default you must also send AT&W (this page has no button for it; hand-type it on the command line if needed).

Making error messages readable (CMEE)

ButtonEffect
Verbose Err
AT+CMEE=2		 Error codes become text descriptions. Example: with GNSS not yet fixed, numeric mode returns +CME ERROR: 516, text mode returns DSAT_CME_GNSS_NOT_FIXED_NOW — the latter tells you what happened without a lookup table. This tool strongly recommends clicking it right after the power-up ritual
Numeric Err
AT+CMEE=1		 Error codes as numbers — the tool automatically looks up the code and annotates it
Both settings are session-only: gone once the modem restarts (a page reload = RTS power cut = a restart, which also counts). Also found in testing: even with CMEE=2 on, a few subsystems (such as file-system FILE errors) still emit a mix of text and numbers — a parser must accept both forms.

AT&F: back to factory defaults — the scope

The Factory Reset button resets the AT settings to factory values, the first step when taking over a module someone has misconfigured. It is the only button on this page that asks for confirmation first. Scope confirmed by testing: it sets echo back to on (the echo toggle button's state follows automatically) and does not affect the baud rate; whether each remaining setting is restored, check item by item under the AT&F entry in the manual.

The SIM triple check: is it there, is it waiting for a password, how far has it initialized

ButtonThe question it asksHow to read it
Card In?
AT+QSIMSTAT?		 Is the card seated properly The reply has two fields: the first is the insert/remove URC switch, the second is the card state — do not read the wrong field. On this unit this button has a record of false reports; see the warning below
SIM PIN
AT+CPIN?		 Is the card waiting for a password +CPIN: READY = "not currently waiting for any password". ⚠ It does not mean this card needs no PIN — a PIN-protected card also returns READY once unlocked. With no card it returns +CME ERROR: 10
Init State
AT+QINISTAT		 Initialization progress A bitmask: 1 = CPIN ready, 2 = SMS, 4 = phonebook, 7 = all done. Measured on this unit once boot settles: 3 (phonebook bit never set) — to decide "can I start", bit 1 is enough; do not wait forever for 7
Card In? lies on this unit. Measured: AT+QSIMSTAT? returned 0,0 (card removed), yet at the same moment CPIN was READY, the network attached, and an IP obtained — the card was perfectly fine. Presumably the control board does not wire the SIM_DET detect pin (or AT+QSIMDET is not enabled), so the reading is permanently "not inserted". To decide whether the card is present, trust AT+CPIN? or AT+QINISTAT.

Whose card is this: IMSI and ICCID

The IMSI button (AT+CIMI) returns a string of bare digits, the card's subscriber identity on the mobile network. Measured on this unit: 901405117661468 — the first three digits (MCC) are 901 = the international roaming number range. This unit's card is a 1NCE IoT SIM, which also explains why AT+CEREG? keeps returning 0,5 (registered, roaming): not a signal anomaly, but the norm for this kind of card. Recognize a roaming card before running data tests, and mind the data pricing.

The ICCID button (AT+QCCID) queries the card's serial number; measured reply +QCCID: 89882280666176614687. ⚠ The manual has no AT+CCID command — the one common in other vendors' modem tutorials does not work here; use Quectel's own AT+QCCID.

PIN unlocking: check the remaining attempts first, then act

  1. Click PIN Left first (AT+QPINC?) to see the remaining attempts — the manual's ranges: PIN 0–3 attempts left, PUK 0–10 attempts left. Know how many shots you have before you act.
  2. When the card is waiting for a PIN, click Enter PIN: it first expands a parameter card for you to fill in the PIN before sending (command template AT+CPIN="{pin}", waits up to 5 seconds).
  3. When the PIN attempts are exhausted and the card demands a PUK, click Unlock PUK: the manual requires the PUK to be sent together with a new PIN (AT+CPIN="{puk}","{newpin}"), likewise via the parameter card, waiting up to 5 seconds.
Every wrong attempt costs one; when the PUK runs low, stop and contact the carrier — do not burn through the attempts by guessing.

The three status buttons: clock, voltage, network time

ButtonWhat it showsMeasured values and how to read them
Clock
AT+CCLK?		 The module's RTC clock +CCLK: "26/08/01,00:55:32+32". The time-zone field +32 is in quarter-hours (15 minutes): 32 × 15 min = UTC+8. Measured on this unit, the RTC had already been synced by the network; time and zone both correct
Battery
AT+CBC		 Supply voltage Some firmware does not support it and an ERROR reply is normal; this unit's firmware does — measured +CBC: 0,0,4264, where the last field is the voltage (mV), i.e. 4.264 V
Net Time
AT+QLTS=2		 Current local time derived from network sync Measured +QLTS: "2026/08/02,11:46:47+32,0". The difference from Clock is the source: CCLK reads the module's own RTC, QLTS takes the network time directly; the year format also differs (RTC two digits, QLTS four) — do not confuse them when parsing

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
Querying the SIM right after RDY returns error 14 or 13 The SIM is still initializing (14 = SIM busy; 13 = SIM failure has also appeared at this stage). Wait about 6 seconds and resend — do not rush to declare the card dead
Card In? says the card was removed, yet everything else works A SIM_DET detect-pin issue (measured case on this unit), not a card problem. Look at AT+CPIN? / AT+QINISTAT instead
Every character appears twice on screen Module echo and the terminal's local echo are both on — one click of the echo toggle button fixes it
Errors come back as cold bare numbers CMEE is not on yet. Click Verbose Err; it is session-only and must be re-clicked after every power-up ritual
Commands go out and get no response at all Reopening the port re-asserts RTS = a power cut; the module has in fact rebooted. You must rerun the full power-up ritual — skip it and nothing responds

Network — Registration, operators, RF

Working principle: every data feature works only if the module is registered on the cellular network and the PDP data channel is ready — this page is the dashboard and switchboard for getting on the network, and every "cannot get online" investigation starts here. All numbers in this section were measured on a physical EG800K in August 2026.

Before you start: switch URCs to the UART first

From the factory, the EG800K sends its unsolicited messages (URCs) to usbat (the USB AT port), while this tool uses the UART — so not a single URC gets through: signal reports, TCP / MQTT / Wi-Fi scan results all go silent, and the symptom is "every command replies OK, but no messages ever come".

This is the number-one cause of "all URCs vanished". Go to the Hardware tab, query with AT+QURCCFG="urcport", and if it is not "uart1", switch it with the toggle button — the setting is written to NVRAM; change it once and it survives reboots.

Step one: confirm the registration state

After the power-up ritual shows RDY, click AT+CEREG? first (the most accurate one on a 4G module). The three registration buttons map to three domains: CEREG = LTE/EPS, CREG = circuit-switched domain, CGREG = packet-switched domain; the second number (stat) reads the same for all:

statMeaningWhat to do
0Not registered yetCommon right after boot; wait a few seconds and query again
1Registered (home network)Normal, proceed
2SearchingWait
3Rejected by the networkCheck the SIM / plan; use CEER for the reason
5Registered (roaming)The normal state on this unit, see below
stat=5 is not a fault. Measured: all three registration queries return 0,5 — the SIM is a 1NCE IoT card (MCC 901, an international roaming card) that counts as "roaming" in any country; treat 5 as 1.

If registration succeeds but you still cannot get online, click AT+CGATT? next to check packet-domain attach; if needed, click AT+CGATT=1 to attach manually, and on failure use AT+CEER for the reason (a different layer from the TCP/IP page's QIGETERROR). CGATT can block up to 140 seconds — do not hammer it.

Which operator and which band are you on right now

AT+COPS? queries the currently registered operator (a trailing 7 = LTE). Trap: the operator name may be an empty string — measured reply +COPS: 0,0,"",7, not a fault. To see the operator, click AT+QNWINFO instead (technology / operator / band / channel):

+QNWINFO: "FDD LTE","46692","LTE BAND 8",3750

46692 = Chunghwa Telecom, Band 8; with no service it returns NO SERVICE. This roaming card picks its own network: on different days it was measured on Chunghwa Telecom Band 8 and on FarEasTone (466-01) Band 3 — switching operator and band is all normal. AT+COPS=? scans every operator in the area: it can block up to 300 seconds and interrupts ongoing services; click it only if you really need it.

Signal strength and quality: CSQ is only a rough figure

AT+CSQ returns rssi and ber: rssi 0–31 maps to -113 to -51 dBm, 99 = undetectable (common right after boot; wait a few seconds). Measured rssi 18–24 (-77 to -65 dBm, good); ber is permanently 99, no reference value. LTE's real quality trio — RSRP (strength) / RSRQ (quality) / SINR (signal-to-noise ratio; low = interference) — is available only through the Signal URC group (AT+QINDCFG="sqi" with no value = query the switch):

ButtonCommandEffect
LTE QualityAT+QINDCFG="sqi",1 Enables RSRP / RSRQ / SINR reporting — indispensable for antenna and placement tests. It only pushes when the signal "changes"; if nothing happens, cup the antenna or unplug/replug it. The setting does not survive reboots
Signal PushAT+QINDCFG="csq",1 Reports whenever the signal changes, replacing frantic CSQ clicking
URC Off / OnAT+QINDCFG="all",0 / 1 One-click mute when you are being flooded — remember to turn it back on afterwards

The PDP channel: the 3GPP layer vs the TCP/IP page

A PDP context = the "data channel" the cellular network allocates; only with it do you have an IP. This group is read-only queries at the 3GPP standard layer: AT+CGDCONT? lists contexts and APNs, AT+CGACT? lists activation states (blocks up to 150 seconds; ⚠ the write form takes its parameters in the opposite order), and AT+CGPADDR lists the obtained IPs. The TCP/IP page's QIACT? / QICSGP are Quectel's own stack — not the same layer — and comparing them side by side tells you which side is broken: an IP here but none over there = the network granted it but the stack never started. This unit auto-activates a PDP and obtains an IP at boot.

AT+QGDCNT? queries cumulative data usage (first number sent, second received) — a must when metering a roaming card. ⚠ Testing overturns the button hint's "accumulates across reboots": by default the counter is not saved to NV and resets to zero on any power cut (page reloads included) — record it on the spot, or save to NV with AT+QGDCNT=1.

Field debugging: this card allows only a single PDP

Clicked AT+QIACT=1 on the TCP/IP page and got ERROR (572,operation not allowed)? This card's fixed script: after boot the 3GPP layer has already auto-activated one PDP, but the context number drifts (both 1 and 9 seen in testing); opening a second one returns +CME ERROR: 100 ⇒ the network allows only a single PDP; and QIACT's contextID range is only 1–8, so when the PDP lands on 9 the Quectel stack cannot touch it at all. The two-step fix (do it once after every boot):

AT+CGACT?             ← see which cid it is (the number drifts; do not skip this)
AT+CGACT=0,<that cid>   ← the 3GPP layer gives up the slot
AT+QIACT=1            ← TCP/IP page; a reply of +QIACT: 1,1,1,"10.187.7.8" means success

Setting the APN with QICSGP can be skipped on this card — measured, the module auto-syncs the network-assigned APN (iot.1nce.net); it becomes necessary only with enterprise APN cards that need credentials.

Everything suddenly timing out mid-test? Suspect PDP drift first. Measured: while HTTP failed continuously (error 716, fixed 30-second timeouts), AT+QIACT? still returned an IP — at that moment it lies, so cross-check against AT+CGACT? (measured: 1,0 and 9,1 = drifted to 9). Fix: AT+QIDEACT=1 → AT+CGACT=0,<the drifted cid> → AT+QIACT=1, then verify with a ping.

CFUN functionality levels and RF control

The whole RF Control group changes the module's state; every button is a red-framed confirm-before-click one. Click AT+CFUN? first to see the current level before acting:

CommandLevelMeaning
AT+CFUN=1Full functionality RF fully on; always recover with this one
AT+CFUN=4Airplane TX/RX fully off, SIM still active — the starting point for "re-registration" tests
AT+CFUN=0Minimum SIM disabled too; the manual only says Minimum functionality without details
AT+CFUN=1,1Soft restart Restarts the whole module. ⚠ The AT port goes dead briefly; wait for RDY again

CFUN can block up to 15 seconds. If the SIM has a PIN lock, after switching back to CFUN=1 you must re-enter the PIN before it registers. AT+CGATT=0 (PS Detach) leaves the packet domain — it kills every TCP / MQTT connection; use it only to test "re-attach".

Advanced: QENG reads the serving cell (command-line input)

This page has no button for it — type AT+QENG="servingcell" on the command line to read the serving cell's parameters. Key fields as measured:

FieldMeasured valueHow to read it
MCC / MNC466 / 01Taiwan / FarEasTone
Cell ID / TACABCDE02 / 1234 (hex) Decimal 180149762 / 4660; eNodeB = ECI≫8 = 703710, sector = 2
PCID / EARFCN144 / 1550 Physical cell ID (not globally unique) / Band 3
RSRP / RSRQ / RSSI / SINR-113 / -18 / -92 / -1 RSRP below -100 counts as poor; SINR -1 dB = poor quality
Cell ID and TAC are hexadecimal; convert to decimal before querying any database. Databases like OpenCelliD only take decimal — throwing ABCDE02 at them just returns no match. Also, AT+QENG="neighbourcell" returns only PCIDs, no global Cell ID (an LTE standard limitation).

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
Commands all reply OK, unsolicited messages never appear urcport is on usbat (the factory value) — switch to uart1 on the Hardware tab
QIACT=1 returns ERROR (572) The single PDP slot is taken — walk through the two-step fix above
Consecutive requests all time out at a fixed 30 seconds PDP drift — cross-check with AT+CGACT?; do not trust QIACT? alone

GNSS — Satellite positioning

Working principle: GNSS is a feature independent of the mobile network — it needs no data plan on the SIM, no PDP, and consumes no data (AGNSS excepted, see below). Once enabled, the module receives satellite signals on its own, and you poll for a fix with AT+QGPSLOC. Every timing and behavior in this section is a value measured on a physical EG800K in August 2026.

Before you start: the antenna decides everything

The number-one cause of failed fixes is not a mistyped command; it is an antenna that receives no signal. Measured comparison: indoors with a poor antenna, the module could list the positions of 38 satellites yet hear not a single one (SNR all 00); after switching to an active GNSS antenna placed by a window, a cold start got a fix within 95 seconds.

You cannot test GNSS indoors — no amount of waiting will help. With no sky view, $GNGGA reports "satellites used 00, fix quality 0", and AT+QGPSLOC forever returns error 516. Move the antenna to a window or outdoors before you start — this is not a patience problem, it is a physics problem.

Your first fix: five steps

  1. Run the power-up ritual (see the Power-Up Ritual section). ⚠ Every page reload equals a power cut: the GNSS on/off state and any half-received ephemeris are wiped, and you start over from this step.
  2. Confirm URCs go to the UART: AT+QURCCFG="urcport" must return "uart1". The factory value is "usbat"; left unchanged, many result messages get sent to the USB port and never show up here (the setting is written to NVRAM, so change it once and you are done).
  3. Turn GNSS on: click AT+QGPS=1. Within a few seconds you will see +QGPS: "firmware",0,0 (GNSS firmware loaded successfully). Clicking it again while already on returns +CME ERROR: 504, which is harmless.
  4. Check reception: click AT+QGPSGNMEA="GSV" to read the visible satellites. The terminal area automatically opens the Satellites tab and draws the signal-strength bar chart and sky view — how to read them is covered in the next section.
  5. Poll for a fix: click AT+QGPSLOC=2 every 5–10 seconds. A reply of DSAT_CME_GNSS_NOT_FIXED_NOW (error 516) means no fix yet — just keep waiting. On success it returns coordinates, and the terminal area automatically opens the Map tab and plots the position.

Reading the Satellites tab: "in view" does not mean "heard"

GSV gives four numbers per satellite: ID, elevation, azimuth, and SNR (signal-to-noise ratio, dB-Hz). The first three only say "where in the sky it should be"; only the SNR proves a signal is actually being received.

SNRMeaning
(blank) or 00Nothing received at all — you know where it is, but you cannot hear it
14–28Marginal: ephemeris demodulation keeps failing and restarting; fixes are slow and unstable
30 and aboveDemodulates reliably; once most satellites reach this level, the fix comes quickly
40 and aboveThe level of open sky plus a good antenna

Why you must wait: the physics of a cold start, with measured times

A fix needs each satellite's precise orbit (the ephemeris), and the ephemeris is buried in a signal the satellite broadcasts at 50 bps — one satellite takes about 18–30 seconds of continuous error-free demodulation, a single bad bit means starting over, and you need at least 4 of them. That is why a "cold start" is slow. Measured on this unit (same location, active antenna, measurement resolution ±5 seconds):

ScenarioTime to first fix (measured)
Cold start (no assistance at all)95 seconds
Cold start + AGNSS52 seconds (and a rough position already comes back after about 20 seconds)
AGNSS + recent leftover ephemeris (day-to-day repeated use)25 seconds
Do not reload the page while testing. This tool's hardware design makes RTS = power, so reloading the page = a power cut = all ephemeris lost, and everything restarts from a cold start. To pause, click AT+QGPSEND; do not cut power.

AGNSS acceleration: the full procedure

Principle: AGNSS switches the ephemeris to a network download (about 32–34 KB each time), skipping the slow 50 bps demodulation. It cannot conjure satellite signal out of nothing — indoors you still get no fix; all it saves is the "waiting for the ephemeris" time.

Two prerequisites are the easiest to miss, and missing either one makes AGNSS silently do nothing at all, with no error:

PrerequisiteCommandTrap
AGNSS enabledAT+QAGPS=1 ⚠ Takes effect only after a reboot (written to NVRAM; set it once and you are done)
PDP activeAT+QIACT=1 ⚠ Must be re-sent after every boot. AT+CGATT? returning 1 does not count — attach is only network-layer registration; only when AT+QIACT? can return +QIACT: 1,1,…,"IP" do you have a data channel

The full sequence (after every boot):

AT+QIACT=1          ← open the data channel (blocks up to 150 seconds; consumes data)
AT+QIACT?           ← must show +QIACT: 1,1,…,"IP"
AT+QGPS=1           ← turn GNSS on; AGNSS downloads its assistance data automatically at this point
AT+QGPSLOC=2        ← poll every 5–10 seconds

How do you confirm AGNSS is actually working? This unit's firmware does not emit any notification like +QGPS: "agps" (confirmed by testing), so you look for circumstantial evidence — any one of these three will do:

  1. Query AT+QGDCNT? twice, before and after AT+QGPS=1; about 30 KB more in the receive direction = the assistance data was downloaded
  2. GSV lists the positions of a large number of satellites within seconds (SNR possibly still 00) — the positions were downloaded; demodulating them yourself could never be that fast
  3. The time field of $GNGGA has a value (time is part of the assistance data too)
The fake-fix trap: coordinates with zero satellites are not a fix. About 20 seconds after AGNSS starts, AT+QGPSLOC may return a set of coordinates, but look closely: HDOP 0.00 / alt 0.0 / nsat 00 — that is the reference-position injection from the assistance data, not a measurement, and it can be far off.

The criteria for a real fix: satellites used > 0, fix mode ≥ 2, HDOP > 0. Automation or product logic must never rely on "did coordinates come back" alone.

apflash: fast even after a power cut (with conditions)

AT+QGPSCFG="apflash" is 1 from the factory: every successful fix saves the ephemeris to flash, and the next boot imports it automatically — power-cycle within an hour and a cold start becomes a fast hot start, at zero data cost. Two limits: the ephemeris expires in roughly an hour; and you must have gotten a fix at least once before flash has anything to import — on a module that has never fixed, apflash cannot help.

After the fix: the Map tab

Every successful AT+QGPSLOC plots the position on the Map tab: the blue marker is the latest position, the cyan line is the movement track, and hovering over any track point shows local time and altitude. The summary bar shows coordinates / altitude / HDOP / satellite count, with the time converted to the local time zone by longitude.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
+CME ERROR: 505 GNSS is not on yet — send AT+QGPS=1 first. It must be turned on again after every reboot (page reloads included)
+CME ERROR: 504GNSS is already on; you merely enabled it twice. Harmless
Error 516 (NOT_FIXED_NOW) No fix yet. If GSV shows signal (SNR ≥ 30), keep waiting; if everything is 00 it is an antenna/environment problem, and no amount of waiting will help
No continuous NMEA stream The factory outport is usbnmea, so the continuous stream goes to the USB port. On the AT port just grab sentences one at a time with AT+QGPSGNMEA (requires nmeasrc,1 first; the button on this page has it covered)
AT+QGPSDEL to force a cold start ⚠ Do not use it — this unit's firmware answers =? with (0-2) yet rejects all three parameters (INVALID_PARA), and the official manual does not document it either. For a real cold start: apflash,0 plus a power cycle (remember to set it back to 1 after testing)
A changed setting does not take effect QAGPS takes effect only after a reboot; so does gnssconfig (the constellation mix). After changing them, run the power-up ritual once

TCP/IP — The root of every data connection

Working principle: this page is the foundation of every data protocol. The PDP context (the data channel allocated by the cellular network) is activated and deactivated only on this page; the SSL / HTTP / MQTT / FTP pages carry read-only queries only, so the same command never gets driven from two places at once. All traps and timings in this section were measured on the real device in August 2026.

Step one: activate the PDP (QICSGP / QIACT / QIDEACT)

Click Act PDP (AT+QIACT=1): it can block up to 150 seconds — send no other commands meanwhile — and from here on data charges begin (mind roaming costs). After success always click Query IP (AT+QIACT?) and confirm it returns +QIACT: 1,1,1,"IP address" — before activation it returns only OK. To hang up, click Deact PDP (AT+QIDEACT=1, up to 40 seconds), which force-closes every connection under it. Set APN (AT+QICSGP) is normally unnecessary — the module auto-syncs the network-assigned APN (measured: the 1NCE card already read back iot.1nce.net at boot); only enterprise APNs with credentials need it.

Act PDP returns ERROR, Last Error 572? This card allows only one PDP. At boot the network has already auto-activated one, and its number drifts (both 9 and 1 seen in testing), while AT+QIACT can only reach 1–8. Fix: on the Network page, AT+CGACT? to find the number → AT+CGACT=0,<number> to give up the slot → click Act PDP again.

Everything dies mid-test? AT+QIACT? lies — during PDP drift it still returns an IP; only a cross-check against AT+CGACT? reveals it. Recovery: Deact PDP → AT+CGACT=0,<drifted number> → Act PDP → verify with Ping.

Opening a connection: OK only means "command accepted"

Click Open TCP and fill host and port in the parameter card (AT+QIOPEN=1,0,"TCP","host",port,0,0; context 1, connectID 0 and buffer mode are fixed). OK only means the command was accepted; success or failure comes in the URC +QIOPEN: 0,<err>: 0 = success, up to 150 seconds; 563 = the connectID is still open — click Close Sock first. All Socks (AT+QISTATE) lists every socket; state 2 = connected.

Sending data: three ways

ButtonDescription
Send Text
AT+QISEND=0,<len>		 Fixed-length two-stage: wait for >, then send the payload; the length is computed automatically, no Ctrl+Z needed. First choice for plain text; limit 1460 bytes, supports \n \r \t \xHH escapes
The three Send Var buttons
AT+QISEND=0		 Variable-length: enters data mode and keeps receiving until Ctrl+Z (0x1A) sends it off — can be written in installments, see the next paragraph
Send Hex
AT+QISENDEX=0,"hex"		 Single-line, no data mode. Can send arbitrary bytes (0x00 included); hex limit 512 characters = 256 actual bytes

Send (append): the first click enters data mode, each later click appends another chunk (while already in data mode the command is not re-sent — re-sending it would become data); Send then auto-finish appends and adds the Ctrl+Z, fastest when sending a single chunk; Finish (Ctrl+Z) sends the accumulated content in one go. The terminal flags data mode while you are in it; to abandon, click ESC Cancel (0x1B, the escape key when a two-stage command jams). ⚠ The data must not contain 0x1A (it would be taken as an early finish); for control characters use Send Hex instead.

SEND OK does not mean the peer received it — only that the data was handed to the module. Click Check ACK (AT+QISEND=0,0) to see sent / ACKed; only acked counts.

Receiving data: it does not appear by itself — click Read Data

In buffer mode, received data does not appear in the terminal on its own: the module only issues a +QIURC: "recv",0 notice, and you must click Read Data (AT+QIRD=0,1500) to fetch it, repeating until it returns +QIRD: 0 — until the buffer is drained there will be no next notice. Unread Len (AT+QIRD=0,0) shows total received / read / unread. When done, click Close Sock (AT+QICLOSE=0, up to 10 seconds). ⚠ No recv notices at all? On the Hardware page check whether AT+QURCCFG="urcport" is uart1 — the factory value is the USB port, and all URCs go there.

The two quirks of the built-in peer tcpbin.com

Open TCP's default peer is the free echo server tcpbin.com:4242, with two measured quirks:

  • Line-by-line echo; the line must end with a newline (0A): Hello without 0A got no reply after 6 seconds; with the 0A added, the echo arrived in 0.1 seconds. Append \n with Send Text, or a trailing 0A with Send Hex.
  • 15-second idle timeout: idle connections get dropped with a +QIURC: "closed",0. This has nothing to do with QIRD (it only reads the local buffer, it never touches the network). To keep the connection, send real data at least every 10 seconds. After closed, the socket sits in closing — you must click Close Sock first before reuse, or QIOPEN returns 563.

The diagnostic trio: Ping / DNS Lookup / NTP Sync

Button (all require Act PDP first)Behavior and measurements
Ping
AT+QPING		 Timeout 4 seconds ×4, fixed. Measured: 8.8.8.8 all through, RTT 160–270 ms. ⚠ Many servers block ICMP — a failed ping does not mean TCP cannot connect; for reachability just Open TCP
DNS Lookup
AT+QIDNSGIP		 Results come back as the URC +QIURC: "dnsgip" (up to 60 seconds); measured: arrives in two parts, with multiple IPs
NTP Sync
AT+QNTP		 Up to 125 seconds, port 123 fixed; the result comes in the URC +QNTP. ⚠ The time is UTC yet carries a local time-zone tag (+32 quarter-hours = GMT+8; measured exactly 8 hours off); for local time use AT+CCLK?

When it goes wrong: click Last Error first, then the 30-second triage

The moment a command returns ERROR, click Last Error (AT+QIGETERROR) immediately — only the last one is kept, and once the next error overwrites it, it is gone. It queries the Quectel stack layer; for the network layer use the Network page's AT+CEER.

🔴 Data-stack degradation — the most time-consuming pit. Symptom: every connection fails, yet every self-check says all is well (QIACT? has an IP, QIGETERROR returns 0). Measured: triggered after about 20 consecutive SSL open/close cycles, after which even plain-TCP QIOPEN returned 552; QIDEACT + QIACT cannot save it — only rerunning the power-up ritual recovers.

The 30-second triage: hit the same target with Open TCP — if that fails too, the whole stack is broken, rerun the power-up ritual; if it succeeds, the problem is in the upper protocol — keep digging.

Keepalive: holds off carrier NAT, cannot hold off tcpbin

QICFG=? lists the sub-items and ranges, Keepalive? reads the current value, Keepalive On / Off toggles it — these four commands themselves cost zero data; once enabled, as long as any socket sits idle, the probe packets count against your mobile data. It cannot hold off tcpbin's 15-second timeout: measured, even enabled, the drop still came at 15.1 seconds — keepalive is a TCP-layer empty probe invisible to the application; and the minimum interval is 25 seconds, already larger than 15. To survive an application-layer timeout you must send real data (e.g. Send Hex a 0A every 10 seconds). Its real purpose is carrier NAT keep-alive (IoT-card NAT entries get reclaimed after a few idle minutes).

The data bill (estimated, not measured): one probe round trip is about 80 bytes; default idle = 30 seconds of continuous idling → about 9.4 KB per hour, about 225 KB per day, about 6.8 MB per month; idle = 600 seconds → about 11 KB per day. Prepaid total-volume cards like 1NCE should raise the idle value. With no socket open, it costs nothing at all.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
+QIOPEN: 0,563 The connectID is still open — Close Sock first
No +QIURC: "recv" arriving ① urcport is not uart1 (Hardware page) ② you never read down to +QIRD: 0, so notices are suppressed
A +QIURC: "closed",0 pops up tcpbin's 15-second idle timeout; reopen after Close Sock
Two-stage command jammed, AT port unresponsive Click ESC Cancel to escape; failing that, Reset on the Hardware page
All connections fail but every self-check is green Data-stack degradation — triage, then rerun the power-up ritual
Act PDP returns ERROR, or everything dies mid-test The single PDP slot is taken / PDP drift — see the two debugging boxes under "Step one"

MQTT — IoT messaging

Working principle: MQTT is a "broker" (message-intermediary server) protocol: devices never connect to each other directly; each connects to the broker and publishes or subscribes to messages on "topics". On the EG800K it is two-layered: first AT+QMTOPEN opens the "network connection" (TCP to the broker), then AT+QMTCONN performs the "MQTT login"; only with both layers up can you subscribe and publish. Remember first: every MQTT command's result follows the "OK first, URC later" pattern (same as FTP) — OK only means the command was accepted; success or failure comes in the result URC that follows.

This page always uses client 0; the firmware also supports multiple clients (0–5), SSL and cloud-platform authentication (confirmed by testing with =?) — see the MQTT application note for advanced usage.

Before you start: two prerequisites

  1. URCs must go to the UART: AT+QURCCFG="urcport" must return "uart1". The factory value is "usbat", and MQTT's results are all URCs — leave it unchanged and every command replies only OK with no follow-up (the Basic page has a button for it; written to NVRAM, change it once).
  2. The PDP must be active first: click AT+QIACT=1 on the TCP/IP page first (up to 150 seconds); without it, +QMTOPEN returns 3 = PDP activation failed. The whole run consumes mobile data, estimated at about 5 KB.

How to test: four free public brokers

The AT+QMTOPEN parameter card has a built-in broker dropdown (free typing still allowed); all four allow anonymous access, no registration. Numbers measured in August 2026 (PC-side burst of 100 messages, module-side ping):

BrokerBurst of 100Module-side pingNotes
mqttgo.io (default)100/100 190–210 msTaiwan HiNet; 1883 plaintext / 8883 TLS
broker.hivemq.com100/100Blocks ICMP Do not panic when AT+QPING returns 559 — measured, TCP 1883 was open on all four; test reachability directly with AT+QMTOPEN
test.mosquitto.org100/100385–400 ms Its own site says not for anything important; worst topic pollution
broker.emqx.io40/100Blocks ICMP Has a publish rate limit; offers a web Dashboard

All four are completely public: anyone can subscribe to your topics, and other people's messages may drift into yours — exactly the problem the random suffix solves.

The random suffix on client ID and topic: a new one on every page reload

The client ID and default topic are not hard-coded: at page load a 6-hex-character suffix is generated, forming numodem-<suffix> and test/numodem-<suffix>; the Subscribe / Publish / Unsub buttons share the same set (otherwise the loopback would not line up). Two reasons:

  • An ID collision gets you kicked off: MQTT 3.1.1 §3.1.4 requires the broker to kick the earlier connection — two people on the same fixed ID kick each other, and the symptom looks like "the module drops for no reason".
  • A fixed topic receives other people's messages: you think you received your own message when you did not — worse than receiving nothing, because it hands you a false pass.
⚠ Every page reload rolls a new suffix — subscribing and publishing must happen within the same page lifetime. Besides, in this tool RTS = power, so a page reload = module power cut: the whole MQTT connection vanishes, and you start over from the power-up ritual and AT+QMTOPEN.

The full walkthrough: connect → subscribe → publish → receive your own message back

The most convincing verification is the loopback: subscribe, publish to the same topic, and receive your own message back — one pass validates the entire send/receive chain. Wait for each step's result URC before moving on:

  1. Set the protocol version: click Ver 3.1.1 (AT+QMTCFG="version",0,4; 3 = 3.1, 4 = 3.1.1). Version? queries the current value (no value = query). The Keepalive parameter card can adjust the keep-alive interval; testing works without touching it.
  2. Open the network: click Open Net (AT+QMTOPEN=0,"broker",1883). It replies OK first; success or failure comes in the URC +QMTOPEN: 0,<result> (0 = success), waiting up to 120 seconds. Open? lists the open connections (with none open it returns an empty OK — measured, normal).
  3. MQTT login: click Connect (AT+QMTCONN=0,"numodem-<suffix>"). The success URC is always +QMTCONN: 0,0,0. Public brokers need no credentials; when credentials are required, append ,"user","pass" to the parameters yourself. Conn? queries the state (1 = initial, 2 = connecting, 3 = connected, 4 = disconnecting).
  4. Subscribe: click Subscribe (AT+QMTSUB=0,1,"test/numodem-<suffix>",0, msgid fixed at 1). The success URC looks like +QMTSUB: 0,1,0,0. From then on, messages on this topic arrive as +QMTRECV URCs.
  5. Publish: click Publish (AT+QMTPUBEX, two-stage, see the next section). The success URC is +QMTPUBEX: 0,<msgid>,0.
  6. Receive it back: the publish target is the topic you are subscribed to, so immediately afterwards you see +QMTRECV carrying the topic and the message body you just sent — loopback successful. Even a Chinese payload arrives untruncated and ungarbled.

QMTPUBEX two-stage: sends automatically once the length is counted out — no Ctrl+Z

The last parameter of AT+QMTPUBEX is the length in bytes, not the message content (settled by MQTT application note §3.3.8 — the single-line form with the message stuffed in always returns ERROR). The correct flow is two-stage: send the command → the module replies with the prompt > → send exactly N bytes, and the module sends automatically once the length is counted out — no Ctrl+Z needed (unlike the data mode of the TCP page's AT+QISEND). The Publish button is fully automatic: just fill the message in the parameter card, and the length is computed from the UTF-8 byte count (one Chinese character = 3 bytes; measured, a two-character Chinese payload → 6).

  • Payload-type commands offer no "insert into command line" — the command line always appends a line ending, and that CR would be counted into the length and shift everything; send with the button.
  • The firmware also has AT+QMTPUB (the data-mode variant, ended with Ctrl+Z) — this tool uses QMTPUBEX throughout, so you need not learn both.

Reading the result codes: every command has its own value range

Never apply command A's result-code table to command B. In +QMTOPEN, 3 means "PDP activation failed"; +QMTPUBEX has no value 3 at all.

The easiest to misread is +QMTCONN: 0,1 — it could be the query response's "state 1 = initializing", or the write result's "packet being retransmitted". A single line cannot tell them apart, so this tool shows both readings side by side instead of guessing.

You need not memorize the tables: for every result URC from +QMTOPEN through +QMTRECV / +QMTSTAT, the terminal area annotates each field in plain language, following the seven reference tables of MQTT application note v1.5.

Going offline and wrapping up

  • Just stop receiving, keep the connection: click Unsub (AT+QMTUNS=0,2,"topic", msgid fixed at 2).
  • Normal disconnect: click Disconnect (AT+QMTDISC=0, sends MQTT DISCONNECT), returning +QMTDISC: 0,0. No need to click Close Net afterwards — AT+QMTCLOSE=0 is for force-closing when "QMTDISC failed and the network layer is stuck".

Disconnects you did not initiate (kicked off, keepalive timeout, network loss) are reported by the +QMTSTAT abnormal-disconnect URC (e.g. +QMTSTAT: 0,5; the terminal area annotates the reason), after which you start over from AT+QMTOPEN.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
Every command replies OK, then nothing URCs are going to the USB port — urcport ships as usbat; switch to uart1 (see prerequisite 1)
+QMTOPEN: 0,3 PDP activation failed — run AT+QIACT=1 first (TCP/IP page), then retry
Subscribed but never receiving your own messages The page was reloaded partway — the suffix rolled and the module also power-cycled. Redo the whole walkthrough within one page lifetime
Receiving messages you did not send Public-broker topic pollution (mosquitto is the worst). The default topic already carries the random suffix; give custom topics distinctive names
Some messages lost during bulk publishing emqx has a publish rate limit (measured: only 40 of a 100 burst arrived) — switch to mqttgo.io or hivemq (100/100, no throttling)
Waiting forever with no result URC This family is simply slow: QMTOPEN up to 120 seconds, QMTCONN / QMTSUB / QMTPUBEX up to 600 seconds (PUBEX = 60-second packet timeout × 10 retries) — the button help marks this; it is not a hang

WiFiScan — Wi-Fi scanning and network positioning

Working principle: the EG800K is an LTE module with no Wi-Fi connectivity, but it carries a built-in "scan-only, never-connect" Wi-Fi receiver: it passively receives the beacon frames broadcast by nearby 2.4GHz hotspots and reports each hotspot's MAC address (BSSID), RSSI (signal strength) and channel. Scanning is pure RF reception at zero data cost; by itself it produces no coordinates — you must send the MAC + RSSI list to a cloud hotspot-location database to trade it for latitude and longitude; that is network positioning, usable indoors, no satellites needed. Every number and behavior in this section was measured on a physical EG800K in August 2026.

The two button groups on this page

The upper half is Wi-Fi Scan, four buttons (pure scanning); the lower half is QuecLocator (QLBS), thirteen buttons (read the reality-check section further down before clicking):

ButtonCommandEffect and measured highlights
Support?AT+QWIFISCAN=? Queries the parameter ranges. This unit actually returns (4000-255000),(1-3),(4-10),(0-255),(0-1)
Read CfgAT+QWIFISCAN? Reads the current parameters. Factory on this unit: 12000,1,5,5,0 = 12-second limit, 1 round, hotspot cap 5, RRC timeout 5 seconds, priority 0
ScanAT+QWIFISCAN Scans once with the current parameters. Results are reported asynchronously after the OK, waiting up to 13 seconds
Scan (custom)Parameter card Scan after customizing time limit (ms) / rounds / hotspot cap / RRC timeout / priority

Your first scan: how to click, what you will see

  1. Run the power-up ritual (see the Power-Up Ritual section).
  2. Confirm URCs go to the UART: AT+QURCCFG="urcport" must return "uart1". The factory value is "usbat" — all scan results get sent to the USB port, and here you see only OK, not even a TIMEOUT (the setting is written to NVRAM; change it once).
  3. Click Scan: the module replies OK first, which means "scan started" — not the result. Within seconds (up to the scan time limit) the results are reported one line at a time, each auto-annotated (MAC / RSSI / channel).

Reading the scan results

A measured report looks like this (2026-08-29, 7 hotspots found, RSSI -37 to -89 dBm):

+QWIFISCAN: (-,-,-37,"C2:28:35:00:00:01",1)
+QWIFISCAN: (-,-,-46,"10:71:B3:00:00:02",4)
+QWIFISCAN: (-,-,-88,"A8:A2:37:00:00:03",6)

The field order is (ecn, ssid, rssi, mac, channel). This unit's firmware always returns - for ecn and ssid (measured 2026-08-02), so the list never shows "whose Wi-Fi this is" — which happens to be enough for positioning: the databases eat MAC + RSSI anyway. RSSI intuition: -30 to -50 very close, -60 to -75 average, below -80 very weak.

When no hotspot is found within the time limit it returns +QWIFISCAN:TIMEOUT — a normal ending, not an error (no space after the colon; this tool's parser handles it). To catch more: use the parameter card to raise the hotspot cap from the factory 5 (this unit's ceiling is 10) and the rounds to 2-3 (measured: results are deduplicated across rounds).

Not every hotspot you catch can be used for positioning. Measured 2026-08-29: of 7 hotspots, 4 were "locally administered addresses" (starting C2: / 62: / 9E:, with the 0x02 bit of the first byte set to 1 — virtual BSSIDs of multi-SSID clones); positioning databases usually ignore such addresses outright, leaving only the 3 global addresses as usable material.
Application note V1.2's parameter ranges are wrong for this unit. The note widens rounds to 1-6 and the hotspot cap to 4-30, but this unit's firmware still actually returns rounds 1-3, hotspot cap 4-10 (measured 2026-08-06). Trust what Support? actually returns; do not copy the note's numbers.

The QuecLocator (QLBS) button group: read the truth before clicking

QuecLocator is Quectel's cloud positioning service: one AT+QLBS command (the Locate button) and the firmware gathers the material itself, sends it to the server for the lookup, and returns coordinates. Three realities:

  1. It needs a token, and it is a paid service. The official document explicitly says to contact Quectel technical support to apply (no self-service signup). This unit's token is empty from the factory.
  2. Not one of the 16 official EG800K documents mentions QuecLocator. The application note on hand is for EC200U / EG915U (syntax and error codes match by testing) — it is not this unit's official document.
  3. This project has ruled it out (2026-08-29): the positioning logic is locked inside the firmware — once the service folds, the whole AT command goes dead and the vendor cannot be swapped (the Quectel forum has confirmed the BG95 series lost support). The buttons remain only for "if a free token ever turns up, verify in passing".
+QLBS: 702 is "server timeout", not a token problem. This project misread 702 as "no token" for three whole weeks — the truth was that the PDP had not been activated first, so the module could not reach the server at all and returned 702 after the full timeout (factory 60 seconds). Controlled experiment 2026-08-29 (token empty throughout): PDP inactive returns 702; once active it returns 10002 (token does not exist) — the server is reachable from Taiwan; the only thing missing is the token. Always run AT+QIACT=1 before AT+QLBS (it consumes data).

All seven configuration sub-items have query / set buttons, and Cfg? (AT+QLBSCFG=?) lists every range in one click (zero data cost). Factory values on this unit and measured highlights:

Sub-item (buttons)Factory valueMeasured highlights
token (Set Token / Token?)empty Reads back always masked as *; the setting path was verified to work
server (Server? / Set Server) www.queclocator.com:80The positioning server address
timeout (Timeout? / Set Timeout)60 seconds The very timeout that 702 waits out; range 10-120
asynch (Async? / Set Async)0 Synchronous / asynchronous switch
latorder (LatOrder?)0 Latitude/longitude output order. ⚠ Set with the lowercase key, but it reads back camel-cased as latOrder
withtime (WithTime?)0 Whether the response carries a time; reads back as withTime
timeupdate (TimeUpd?)0 Whether the fix result corrects the module clock; reads back as timeUpdate

If you actually get a token: fill it in with Set Token → confirm with Token? (shown as *) → activate the PDP on the TCP/IP page → Locate.

The alternative route: token-free network positioning (71 meters measured)

Network positioning does not have to go through QuecLocator. The alternative route was proven end to end on 2026-08-29: the module only produces the material (scan hotspots on this page, read the serving cell with AT+QENG="servingcell"), you save the terminal output to a file and hand it to tools/wifi_geolocate.py, which queries public databases on the PC — zero data cost on the module, no Quectel service. Measured (against the same day's GNSS ground truth): cell-tower lookup via Unwired Labs (free signup) was off by 71 meters (the closing conclusion of this positioning thread); via beaconDB (no key needed), 632 meters; Wi-Fi lookup is stuck on the supplier side — the free ecosystem has collapsed (beaconDB has no coverage in this area, Unwired Labs' free plan excludes Wi-Fi, Google / HERE require a credit card) — shelved.

71 meters is a "lookup hit", not "measurement accuracy". Cell-tower positioning looks up the registered coordinates of that tower by Cell ID, so the same cell always returns the same point — switch towers and the error can jump to kilometer scale; the service's own reported ±1051 meters is the honest estimate. Also, Cell ID and TAC are hexadecimal and must be converted to decimal before the lookup (the tool handles this automatically).

Troubleshooting

Clicking Scan only returns OK; results never appear URCs are going to the USB port — query with AT+QURCCFG="urcport"; if it is not "uart1", change it (written to NVRAM)
+QWIFISCAN:TIMEOUT No hotspot found within the time limit; a normal ending, not an error. Move location or extend the limit
+QLBS: 702 Server timeout — almost always a forgotten AT+QIACT=1, not a token problem
+QLBS: 10002 The token does not exist — it must be bought from Quectel; this project has ruled it out, take the alternative route above

SSL — TLS channels

Working principle: the SSL page is the shared substrate of encrypted connections — the SSL context configured here and the certificates uploaded here serve SSL raw sockets, MQTT over SSL and HTTPS alike. All timings and behavior in this section were measured on a physical EG800K in August 2026.

Your first TLS connection: five steps

  1. Run the power-up ritual (see the Power-Up Ritual section), then click AT+QIACT? to confirm the data channel — it must return +QIACT: 1,1,…,"IP"; if not, run AT+QIACT=1 first.
  2. Configure the context: set sslversion to 4 (all versions, best compatibility), ciphersuite to 0XFFFF (all suites), and seclevel to 0 for now — first prove the channel works; leave verification for later.
  3. Open the connection: click AT+QSSLOPEN (trailing code 0), fill host and port in the parameter card. ⚠ OK only means "command accepted"; success rides on the URC: only +QSSLOPEN: 4,0 is success (measured handshake: 2.0 seconds).
  4. Send data: click AT+QSSLSEND (two-stage) — after the > appears, send the payload; it sends automatically once the declared length is counted out, no Ctrl+Z (single-packet limit 1460 bytes). The peer's reply shows up as +QSSLURC: "recv",4.
  5. Read back and close: AT+QSSLRECV (1500 per read) — reading down to +QSSLRECV: 0 means the buffer is drained, not an error. AT+QSSLCLOSE=4 closes (default wait up to 10 seconds; the other button takes a seconds value, 0 = immediate).
AT+QSSLOPEN=1,1,4,"tcpbin.com",4243,0
OK
+QSSLOPEN: 4,0            ← 2.0 seconds, 0 = success
AT+QSSLSEND=4,15
>
NuModem-P5-SSL            ← sent automatically once 15 bytes are counted out
SEND OK
+QSSLURC: "recv",4        ← 0.4 seconds
AT+QSSLRECV=4,1500
+QSSLRECV: 15
NuModem-P5-SSL
AT+QSSLCLOSE=4

While connected you can click AT+QSSLSTATE to see all connections (=4 queries a single clientID; state 2 = connected). Note that the local port always reads 0 — module behavior, not an error.

The three access modes (AT+QSSLOPEN's trailing code)

CodeBehavior
0 bufferedOn data arrival only +QSSLURC: "recv",<id> is issued; you read it yourself with AT+QSSLRECV
1 direct pushThe URC also carries the length and the data is dumped on the next line; ⚠ in this mode AT+QSSLRECV returning ERROR is normal
2 transparentThe whole AT port becomes the data channel (this page provides buttons for 0 and 1 only)

Context settings, item by item

Unsure which sub-items the firmware supports? Click AT+QSSLCFG=? first — measured, it returns 17 sub-items, more than the application note lists. The common sub-items each have a set and a query button; measured, what is written reads back identically.

Sub-itemFactoryEffect and measured notes
sslversion—Protocol version; 4 = all supported
ciphersuite—Cipher suites; 0XFFFF = all supported
seclevel00 = no verification, 1 = verify the server (requires a CA certificate uploaded first), 2 = mutual authentication (also needs a client certificate + private key)
cacert—CA certificate path, in the form "UFS:filename"; the file must already be in UFS (see the next section)
sni🔴 0 Mandatory for virtual hosts / CDNs — with many domains on one IP, omitting SNI gets you a mismatched certificate and verification always fails with 566
ignorelocaltime🔴 1 From the factory, certificate validity dates are not checked even with seclevel 1. To check them, set 0 — and the module clock must be right
negotiatetime300 Maximum TLS handshake wait in seconds (10–300)
🔴 The three factory defaults together = no certificate verification at all (seclevel 0, sni 0, ignorelocaltime 1); to truly verify, all three must be set right. And these three settings plus cacert do not survive reboots (confirmed by testing) — every boot returns them to factory values; the certificate files in UFS, however, survive power loss.

The UFS file group: how certificates get into the module

UFS is the module's built-in flash storage; measured total capacity 280 KB, each file occupying one 4 KB block. Certificates must be uploaded here first before cacert has a file to point at. Uploads go over the UART at zero data cost, and binary files go through too. The Upload card: after picking a file, the name and size fill in automatically; on submit the tool waits for the module's CONNECT before sending the raw bytes (no CONNECT, nothing is sent). On completion the annotation engine automatically compares the module's reported size and checksum: ✅ = intact, ❌ = corrupted in transit — delete first, then re-upload.

AT+QFUPL="badssl-root.pem",1939,10
CONNECT                   ← now send 1939 bytes
+QFUPL: 1939,4f64         ← received size,checksum; the annotation compares automatically ✅
ButtonPurpose
AT+QFLSTLists every UFS file with its size — use it to verify after upload (zero data cost)
AT+QFLDS="UFS"Queries free / total space in bytes (zero data cost)
AT+QFDELDeletes the named file (* = all); re-uploading without deleting the namesake first gets blocked
Two measured behaviors the manual never spells out: (1) FILE error codes are inconsistent in form — a same-name re-upload returns the text file already exist, a timeout returns the number 421; this tool decodes both. (2) If the size field is larger than the actual file, after the timeout the module still saves what it received as the file — the checksum comparison catches it.

Certificate verification in practice: the paired-test method

Procedure: upload the root certificate → point cacert at it → seclevel 1 → sni 1 → connect to the target's 443. What you upload is the root certificate at the top of the chain (badssl.com's chain has four levels; upload the topmost ISRG Root X1). Testing only "bad certificates fail to connect" is not enough — "nothing connects at all" would also pass. Test in pairs: the good certificate connects and the bad one is refused — it only counts when both directions hold. Measured 2×5 comparison:

Hostseclevel 0seclevel 1
badssl.com (positive control)Connects Connects 4,0
expiredConnectsRefused 566
self-signedConnectsRefused 566
wrong.host (hostname mismatch)ConnectsRefused 566
untrusted-rootConnectsRefused 566

Limitation: all four certificate errors return 566; the module does not distinguish which one it was. AT+QIGETERROR cannot help either — it covers the TCP/IP layer and at this point only returns 0,operate successfully.

For the negative test, avoid expired — the factory ignorelocaltime is 1, so expiry alone is not blocked (it is blocked in the table above only because it also sits outside the uploaded root); for a standalone test use wrong.host. Also watch the data usage: every handshake downloads the full certificate chain, failures included — measured, 30 handshakes cost about 150–200 KB.

🔴 Trap: after about 20 consecutive open/close cycles, the data stack degrades wholesale

Symptom: every AT+QSSLOPEN returns 552 — even seclevel 0 cannot connect, while every self-check says all is well. The 30-second triage: hit the same target with plain-TCP AT+QIOPEN — if that fails too, the data stack is broken; stop auditing SSL settings. A PDP restart cannot save it; only the full power-up ritual recovers. The degradation contaminates test data and is easily misread as "blocked by certificate verification" — reboot to a clean slate before running paired tests.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
+QSSLOPEN: 4,566 Certificate verification failed. Check in order: is sni on (the most common), is cacert's root the right one, is the certificate itself bad; the three settings reset to zero on reboot
Nothing after the OK OK only means accepted; the result comes by URC, waiting up to 150 seconds + negotiatetime
The AT port is stuck and ignores every command AT+QSSLSEND's length was miscounted and it is stuck in data mode swallowing commands — send ESC (0x1B) with the Hardware page's raw-byte button to escape

HTTP — Web requests

Working principle: the module's HTTP is three-phase: first set the URL (a step that is itself two-stage), then issue the request (GET / POST), and finally read the response back. No phase's result lives in the OK; each arrives later as a URC — so AT+QURCCFG="urcport" must be "uart1" (changeable on the Hardware page), or you will see none of the results. All numbers were measured on the real device in August 2026.

Before you start: have a data channel

The prerequisite is an active PDP with an IP (the TCP/IP page's AT+QIACT=1). This page's Connect group holds read-only checks only: AT+CPIN? / AT+CGATT? / AT+CGREG? / AT+QIACT?, AT+QIDNSCFG=1 (DNS 0.0.0.0 = never assigned), AT+QIGETERROR (⚠ valid only for the last TCP/IP command — click it immediately after a failure).

AT+QIACT? lies. Measured: the PDP drifted mid-run — every request failed with error 716 at a fixed 30-second timeout, yet AT+QIACT? kept returning an IP. Cross-check with AT+CGACT?; a mismatch means it drifted. The fix: AT+QIDEACT=1 → AT+CGACT=0,<drifted cid> → AT+QIACT=1, then ping before continuing.

Your first GET: four steps

  1. Preliminary settings (Config group, zero data cost): set the contextid parameter card to 1 (binding the PDP context to use); keep the three switches rspout/auto, requestheader and responseheader at 0 (reasons below); AT+QHTTPCFG? reads back all settings at once for checking, AT+QHTTPCFG=? lists what can be set.
  2. Set the URL (two-stage): the AT+QHTTPURL card has a single "Send (two-stage)" button — you fill in the URL, the length is computed automatically.
